SUPREME COURT OF WESTMARCH

Citation: Marlowe v. Westmarch Licensing Tribunal, 2099 SCC 1

Appeal Heard: November 2, 2098 · Judgment Rendered: March 14, 2099 · Docket: 40123

Between: Elspeth Marlowe, Appellant, and Westmarch Licensing Tribunal, Respondent

Coram: Ashgrove C.J. and Tamsin, Oduya, Ferrante and Lisle JJ.

Reasons for Judgment: (paras. 1 to 11) Ashgrove C.J. (Tamsin, Oduya, Ferrante and Lisle JJ. concurring)

Headnote: Administrative law — Judicial review — Standard of review — Reasonableness — Adequacy of reasons.

I. Overview

[1] This appeal concerns the proper approach to judicial review of a decision of the Westmarch Licensing Tribunal, which cancelled the appellant's licence to operate a ferry service across Lake Corvane.

[2] The appellant, Elspeth Marlowe, held the licence for nineteen years without incident. In 2097, the Tribunal received a complaint that the ferry had departed in unsafe weather. After a hearing, it cancelled the licence under s. 7 of the Ferry Services Act, S.W. 2090, c. F-3.

[3] The Court of Appeal for Westmarch upheld the cancellation, holding that the Tribunal's reasons were adequate and its conclusion reasonable: Marlowe v. Westmarch Licensing Tribunal, 2098 WMCA 44.

[4] For the reasons that follow, I would allow the appeal. The Tribunal did not grapple with the central argument advanced by the appellant, namely that the weather warning had been withdrawn before the ferry departed.

[5] The standard of review is reasonableness. As this Court explained in Vantage Ridge v. Corvane (City), 2096 SCC 12, at para. 85, a reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker.

[6] Reasonableness review is not a line-by-line treasure hunt for error. Nonetheless, a reviewing court must be able to trace the decision maker's reasoning without encountering any fatal flaws in its overarching logic.

[7] Here, the Tribunal wrote:

The licensee has offered various explanations for the departure. We have considered them. The safety of passengers is paramount, and cancellation is warranted.

II. Analysis

[8] With respect, this passage does not engage with the evidence that the warning was withdrawn at 6:40 a.m., twenty minutes before departure. That evidence, if accepted, was capable of answering the complaint entirely.

[9] A decision maker need not respond to every argument. But where an argument is central and, if accepted, would be dispositive, its omission from the reasons may render the decision unreasonable.

[10] The Tribunal's failure to address the withdrawal of the warning is such an omission. Its conclusion therefore lacks the requisite justification, transparency and intelligibility.

[11] I would allow the appeal, set aside the decision of the Court of Appeal, and remit the matter to a differently constituted panel of the Tribunal for redetermination, with costs throughout to the appellant.

Appeal allowed with costs throughout.

Solicitors for the appellant: Fenwick & Rourke, Port Ellery.

1 Ferry Services Act, S.W. 2090, c. F-3, s. 7, was amended in 2097 after the events in issue.

Related documents

  • Zephyr Holdings Ltd. v. Ostrander, 2097 ONCA 412 [1] at paragraph 14 the court considered the standard of review in some depth.
  • R. v. Penhallow, 2096 SCC 9 [2] a related decision about procedural fairness in administrative tribunals.
  • Quinlan v. Board of Tidewater, 2095 FCA 77 [3] considered the same statutory provision.
